title: Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol: Exfiltration Over Unencrypted Non-C2 Protocol
shortTitle: Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol: Exfiltration Over...
summary: This sub-technique is the plaintext branch of exfiltration over an alternative protocol. The parent technique covers sending data over a protocol other than the command and control channel; here the payload is carried without encryption in a protocol that is itself unencrypted, such as unencrypted web, file transfer, or name resolution traffic. The adversary still hides the content, but by encoding or compression rather than cryptography, using widely available schemes such as base64, and by placing data inside protocol fields that are rarely inspected, including headers and query parameters. The result is traffic that passes inspection as ordinary protocol use while carrying a readable payload that any defender who captures and decodes it can immediately understand, which is both the weakness and the investigative opportunity. Because nothing is encrypted, content inspection, proxy logs, and protocol parsing remain effective. Useful artefacts include request sizes and repeated similar requests, uniform resource identifiers with unusually long parameters, file transfer commands with unexpected destinations, encoded strings in proxy or DNS logs, and mailbox or web server records showing uploads of archives from internal hosts. Legitimate automation and software telemetry can produce comparable traffic, so the distinguishing factors are the destination, the account, and whether the host normally performs such transfers.

beginner.definition: This is data theft where the stolen files are sent in a form that is not encrypted. The attacker hides the data by re-encoding it, for example as base64, a way of writing any file using plain letters and numbers. A reader who knows the trick can turn it back into the original file.
beginner.whyItMatters: Unencrypted does not mean harmless, because the data still leaves your network. Encoding hides the content from a quick glance but not from a careful check. These protocols are often allowed through, so the transfer may not be blocked. Logs of web, mail and name requests often keep enough detail to spot it afterwards.
howItWorks: The attacker stages the files and packs them into a single archive to reduce the size.
The archive is re-encoded, for example as base64, so it contains only plain characters.
The encoded text is sent over an unencrypted protocol that the network normally allows.
Data may also be hidden inside header fields, file names or query strings of ordinary requests.
Some transfers are split across many small requests to avoid size based alarms.
On the receiving side the encoded text is decoded back into the original files.
beginner.example: Picture a postcard that must pass through many hands on its way abroad. Anyone who picks it up can read the words, so the sender writes the message in a simple private shorthand instead. Postal workers see a normal postcard, but any curious reader who knows the shorthand learns everything, and the card still reaches its destination.
takeaways: Encoding like base64 is not encryption, and defenders can decode it from captured traffic.
Long encoded strings in web, mail or name request logs are worth reviewing.
Compare outbound volume by host, because unusual senders are easier to spot than unusual protocols.

objectives: Explain how this sub-technique differs from its parent, which covers channel choice rather than payload protection.
Describe encoding and compression as alternatives to encryption for hiding data.
Identify which log sources still capture useful detail when the payload is not encrypted.
Recognise the traffic patterns that indicate bulk data leaving over an unencrypted protocol.
Explain why an unencrypted transfer can still succeed on a network with basic controls.
